one_liner: Pre-alpha JavaScript runtime in Rust (bytecode interpreter today) that starts a hello world about 16x faster than Node and 3x faster than Bun.
what_it_does: katsu is a from-scratch JavaScript/TypeScript engine and runtime in Rust (no V8, JavaScriptCore or QuickJS) invoked as `katsu run file.js`. At 0.1.8 it runs a growing subset of the language (12.31% of test262: objects with shapes, prototype chains, accessors, exceptions, `new`, error constructors, `console.log`, `performance.now`, `String`, `JSON.stringify`) but has no arrays as values the benchmarks can use, no module system, no event loop, no `process`, no filesystem and no garbage collector. It is not a drop-in Node replacement; the planned Node compatibility, baseline JIT, optimizing JIT and AOT-to-Rust mode exist only as specs and milestones.
how_it_is_fast: The startup lead comes from doing almost nothing at startup: a 1.7 MiB Rust executable that loads no non-system shared libraries, a small realm built eagerly at launch (there is no Node bootstrap, no module resolution and no large JavaScript-implemented standard library to instantiate), an oxc-based parser and a register bytecode interpreter. The object model uses NaN-boxed values, shapes that carry the prototype and property flags, a monomorphic per-site inline cache for property reads, and a bump allocator over a 4 GiB compressed-pointer cage with no collector, which is why peak RSS stays near 2.5 MiB. The spec's realm snapshot, resolution cache, bytecode cache and copy-and-patch baseline JIT (Deegen-style, generated from the interpreter description) are planned, not built; crates/katsu-jit/src/lib.rs is a 61-line stub of enums and constants.
when_to_use: Studying how a Rust JavaScript engine is being designed: the spec/ directory (18 documents) and the per-release benchmark write-ups are unusually candid about costs, losses and noise.
Tracking the cold-start and footprint floor of a minimal JS runtime: about 1.5-1.7 ms spawn-to-exit and 1.7 MiB on disk on an Apple M4, against Bun at about 5 ms and Node at about 25 ms.

Reusing the companion harness tamnd/katsu-bench (MIT OR Apache-2.0) to measure cold start, idle RSS, distribution size and checksummed compute workloads across Node, Bun and Deno; it is more careful than most runtime shoot-outs (wait4 peak RSS, IQR-overlap 'too close to call' verdicts, load average recorded).
when_not_to_use: Any real program: no module system, event loop, filesystem, `process`, `Buffer` or npm compatibility; most of test262 fails (12.31% passes at 0.1.8).
Compute: fib(35) is 16-25x slower than Node and Bun (875 ms vs 53.4 ms Node and 34.3 ms Bun at 0.1.6; 781.89 ms vs Bun 33.43 ms at 0.1.8), because there is no JIT yet.

Anything that allocates in a loop: there is no garbage collector, so the heap (a bump allocator over a 4 GiB cage) fills and the process dies (issue #60); the katsu-bench `strings` workload dies this way.
Code that depends on primitive property reads: `'abc'.length` returns undefined rather than 3 without throwing (issue #58, open), a silent wrong answer.

Serverless or CLI cold-start wins on real code: the measured lead is on a one-line hello world and the author expects it to shrink as the runtime gains features (0.1.8 already paid about 0.1 ms for error constructors).

integration.form: standalone CLI binary (GitHub release tarballs; not published on crates.io)
integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond OS libraries (katsu-bench counts only the 1.66 MiB executable); building pulls oxc 0.147, tokio, regress, bumpalo and others from the workspace Cargo.toml
integration.platforms: release binaries for aarch64 and x86-64 macOS, aarch64 and x86-64 Linux (gnu), x86-64 Windows (msvc); all published numbers are from an Apple M4
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded interpreter; the katsu-vm crate docs say an isolate is Send but not Sync
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: `katsu run file.js` executes a one-file script that uses only the implemented subset; no Node modules, APIs or npm packages

gotchas: Filed under JITs but contains no JIT: the measured binary is a bytecode interpreter with a monomorphic inline cache, and crates/katsu-jit/src/lib.rs is a 61-line placeholder (a Tier enum, a tier-up constant and a DeoptReason enum).

Harness detail: katsu-bench's startup axis (src/main.rs measure_axis) ignores --warmup and runs 25 back-to-back spawns per runtime, so 24 of 25 runs see a warm page cache; the 'cold start' median is effectively a warm process start for every runtime (fair across runtimes, but not a true cold start). The katsu-bench README's '25 runs after 3 discarded' applies to the compute workloads, not to startup.

The hello-world peak RSS figures in spec 15.5.1 (katsu 2.44 MiB, Node 48.14, Bun 10.92) came from a separate manual `/usr/bin/time -l` pass that is not in the committed baseline file; results/baselines/2026-08-29-m4-macos.md has no hello-world RSS row, and its idle-memory axis cannot run katsu because katsu exits instead of idling.
Silent wrong answers exist: `'abc'.length` is undefined (issue #58), and a `let` in a `for` head gets one binding per call rather than per iteration (README).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick katsu only to follow or study a from-scratch JS engine's startup and memory floor; for real speed over Node pick Perry (TypeScript AOT, beats Node on compute) or quickjs-jit (a working embeddable JS JIT), and note that XS shows the same 'Node startup dominates' effect on its tiny workloads.
verified_claims_summary: With katsu-bench on an Apple M4 laptop (macOS 15.8, turbo not pinned, 'indicative'), katsu 0.0.5 built with rustc 1.98.0 and fat LTO took a median 1.55 ms (IQR 0.09) to spawn, print one console.log line and exit, against official Bun 1.4.0 at 4.97 ms, Deno 2.9.6 at 12.49 ms and Node 26.8.1 at 24.63 ms (25 back-to-back runs each), with a 1.66 MiB distribution against Node's 139.05 MiB. Later release tarballs hold the lead (0.1.8: 1.68 ms vs Bun 5.67 ms), while the only compute workload katsu can run, fib, is about 23x slower than Bun.
status_note: Active pre-alpha (0.1.8, last commit 2026-08-31, 0 stars, MIT OR Apache-2.0) with release binaries for five targets, but it is a research-stage interpreter with no GC, modules or event loop, so it is reference material rather than something to deploy; the author says the startup lead exists because it does less, not because it is better.
